After seizing power in a 1961 coup, this South Korean army officer ruled as president until his assassination in 1979, presiding over rapid economic growth — who was he?
Park Chung Hee: President of South Korea from 1963 to 1979.
He became king in 2013 when his father abdicated for health reasons, and his eldest daughter, Princess Elisabeth, is now first in line to succeed him — who is he?
Philippe of Belgium: King of the Belgians since 2013.
Known in Hebrew as 'praises,' this anthology of 150 religious hymns is divided into five sections each closing with a doxology — which book of the Bible is it?
Psalms: Book of sacred songs in the Hebrew Bible.
A Bosnian Serb commander of the Army of Republika Srpska during the Yugoslav Wars, he's now serving a life sentence in The Hague for genocide and crimes against humanity — who is he?
This American author built a personal-finance empire around his bestselling Rich Dad Poor Dad book series, even as one of his companies filed for bankruptcy in 2012 — who is he?
Robert Kiyosaki: American finance author and investor (born 1947)
Elected to India's parliament at just 26 — the youngest in the country's history at the time — this Congress politician later served as Rajasthan's deputy chief minister — who is he?
Grand Duke Michael Alexandrovich of Russia
Author of the influential Islamist tract "Milestones," this Egyptian theorist was a leading figure in the Muslim Brotherhood — who is he?
Sayyid Qutb: Egyptian political theorist and revolutionary (1906–1966)
The longest-serving chief minister of Punjab across three separate terms, this politician has twice served as Pakistan's prime minister, most recently since 2024 — who is he?
Shehbaz Sharif: Prime Minister of Pakistan (2022–2023; 2024–present)
Sent to the Ottoman court as a hostage before deserting to lead a league of Albanian noblemen against his former masters, he's remembered as Albania's national hero — who is he?
Skanderbeg: Albanian warlord and military commander (1405–1468)
This retired US Airways pilot safely ditched his disabled airliner on the Hudson River in January 2009 after a bird strike knocked out both engines, saving all 155 aboard — who is he?
Sully Sullenberger: American pilot and diplomat (born 1951)
Rooted in shamanism and animism on the Eurasian steppes and centered on a sky god, this belief system was the state religion of the Mongol Empire — which one?
Tengrism: Religion of the Eurasian steppe nations.
Before ruling Rome from 79 to 81 AD, he commanded the siege that ended the Jewish rebellion — and became the first Roman emperor ever to directly succeed his own biological father; who was he?
Titus: Roman emperor from AD 79 to 81. Titus Flavius Vespasianus (30 December 39 – 13 September 81 AD) was Roman emperor from 79 to 81 AD.
Explicitly authorized by the Constitution, this independent government agency replaced a Cabinet department in 1971 and holds a legal monopoly on traditional letter delivery — which agency?
United States Postal Service: Independent agency of the U.S. federal government.

His brother was executed for revolutionary activities in 1887, pushing him toward radical politics. He founded the Bolsheviks, led the October Revolution, and created the world's first communist state—then ruled it until his death in 1924. Who was this Russian revolutionary?
Vladimir Lenin: Leader of the Soviet Union from 1922 to 1924.
Introduced to the public in 1954 by a retired British civil servant, this modern pagan, Earth-focused religion blends ancient motifs with 20th-century hermetic ideas — which religion?
Wicca: Modern syncretic pagan religion. Wicca draws upon ancient pagan and 20th-century hermetic motifs for theological and ritual purposes.
This 7th-century Chinese Buddhist monk journeyed to the Indian subcontinent from 629 to 645 CE and brought back more than 650 Sanskrit texts to translate — who is he?
Xuanzang: Chinese Buddhist monk and scholar (602–664)
Born into poverty and adopted by a wealthy uncle, this Chinese general commanded the Eighth Route Army and is regarded as a principal founder of the People's Republic. Who was he?
Zhu De: Chinese general and politician (1886–1976)
Which one below was born first?
George Grove (born 1820) is the earliest of the four. Grove was trained as a civil engineer, and successful in that profession, but his love of music drew him into musical administration.
Which of these four is the eldest?
Levi Strauss (born 1829) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these was founded earliest?
Fortran (founded 1957) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four has been around longest?
Earth (formed ~4.54 billion years ago) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these is an astronomer?
Stephen Gray (scientist) is an astronomer. Stephen Gray (December 1666 – February 1736) was an English dyer and astronomer who was the first to systematically experiment with electrical conduction.
Which of these four is a mathematician?
Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen is a mathematician. Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen (born Nicolae Georgescu, 4 February 1906 – 30 October 1994) was a Romanian mathematician, statistician and economist.
What is the atomic number of Dubnium?
Dubnium: Dubnium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Db and atomic number 105.
What is the atomic number of Iridium?
Iridium: Iridium is a chemical element; it has the symbol Ir and atomic number 77.
In what year was B. R. Ambedkar born?
B. R. Ambedkar: Ambedkar served as Law and Justice minister in the first cabinet of Jawaharlal Nehru.
In what year was Hedy Lamarr born?
Hedy Lamarr: Hedy Lamarr (born Hedwig Eva Maria Kiesler; November 9, 1914 – January 19, 2000) was an Austrian and American actress and inventor.
In what year was Erwin Schrödinger born?
Erwin Schrödinger: Schrödinger shared the 1933 Nobel Prize in Physics with Paul Dirac "for the discovery of new productive forms of atomic theory".
In what year did William Howard Taft die?
William Howard Taft: Taft attended Yale and joined Skull and Bones, of which his father was a founding member.
In what year did Karl Marx die?
Karl Marx: Born in Trier in the Kingdom of Prussia, Marx earned a doctoral degree in philosophy from the University of Jena in 1841.
In what year was Fluorine discovered?
Fluorine: Fluorine is a chemical element; it has symbol F and atomic number 9.
Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-15: Russian Aircraft Corporation MiG. The MiG-15 was one of the first successful jet fighters to incorporate swept wings to perform near Mach 1.
Which country is Panavia Tornado from?
Panavia Tornado: Italy. It first flew on 14 August 1974 and was introduced into service in 1979–1980.
Who is credited with discovering Phoenix?
Phoenix (constellation): Petrus Plancius. Named after the mythical phoenix, it was first depicted on a celestial atlas by Johann Bayer in his 1603 Uranometria.
Who is credited with discovering Glycerol?
Glycerol: Carl Wilhelm Scheele. Glycerol is a sugar alcohol with chemical formula C3H5(OH)3.
Who is credited with discovering Theory of relativity?
Theory of relativity: Albert Einstein. Special relativity applies to all physical phenomena in the absence of gravity.
Who is credited with discovering Sombrero Galaxy?
Sombrero Galaxy: Pierre Méchain. It is a member of the Virgo II Groups, a series of galaxies and galaxy clusters strung out from the southern edge of the Virgo Supercluster.
In chemistry, this class is defined by an −OH group that lends water-loving properties to otherwise water-shy hydrocarbons, spanning everything from ethanol to sugar versions — what is it?
Alcohol (chemistry) (from Arabic al-kul 'the kohl') is a type of organic compound that carries at least one hydroxyl (OH) functional group bound to a saturated carbon atom.
Closely related to Hepatica and Pulsatilla, which flowering plant genus in the buttercup family is nicknamed the windflower?
Anemone is a genus of flowering plants in the buttercup family Ranunculaceae.

A German former computer repair technician, this man received international attention after murdering and cannibalizing a voluntary victim he had found over the Internet in March 2001, and was ultimately convicted of murder in a 2006 retrial — who is he?

Armin Meiwes (born 1 December 1961) is a German former computer repair technician who received international attention for murdering and cannibalising Bernd Brandes, whom he had found via the Internet as a voluntary victim, in March 2001.
Only eight species of this stocky-legged, shaggy, short-tailed carnivoran survive, ranging across North and South America and Eurasia — what mammal is it?
Bear are carnivoran mammals of the family Ursidae.
A child prodigy who wrote a treatise on conic sections at 16, which Frenchman later traded letters with Fermat on probability and built early calculating machines?
Blaise Pascal (19 June 1623 - 19 August 1662) was a French mathematician, physicist, inventor, philosopher, and Catholic writer.
This small leafy vegetable, a cultivar of cabbage grown for its edible buds, shares its name with a European capital — what is it?
Brussels sprout is a member of the Gemmifera cultivar group of cabbages (Brassica oleracea), grown for its edible buds.

Honored twice by the American Psychological Association — in 1956 for scientific contributions and 1972 for professional ones — this psychologist championed a person-centered approach to therapy — who is he?
Carl Rogers (January 8, 1902 - February 4, 1987) was an American psychologist who was one of the founders of humanistic psychology and was known especially for his person-centered psychotherapy.

This compound is a yellowish-green gas above 11°C, a reddish-brown liquid when cooler, and bright orange crystals when very cold — usually handled in solution as a bleach and disinfectant. What is it?

Chlorine dioxide is a chemical compound with the formula ClO2 that exists as yellowish-green gas above 11 C (52 F), a reddish-brown liquid between 11 and 59 C (52 and 74 F), and as bright orange crystals below 59 C (74 F).
What's the scientific family name for the group of birds that includes both doves and pigeons — stout-bodied birds with small heads and no formal distinction between the two common names?
Columbidae is a bird family consisting of doves and pigeons.
Mostly aquatic mandibulate arthropods, this group spans shrimp, crayfish, copepods, and barnacles — and modern science now files insects in alongside them — what are they?
Crustacean (from Latin word "crustacea" meaning: "those with shells" or "crusted ones") are mandibulate arthropods that are traditionally a part of the paraphyletic subphylum Crustacea.
A colorless organosulfur compound known as the most widely used commercial sulfoxide, an important polar solvent. It leaves a distinctive taste when absorbed through the skin. What is it?
Dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) is an organosulfur compound with the formula (CH3)2S=O.
Sometimes occurring spontaneously during sleep as a nocturnal emission, this process involves the discharge of semen through the urethra — what is it called?
Ejaculation is the discharge of semen (the ejaculate; normally containing sperm) from the penis through the urethra.
From abortion to animal welfare to business practices, the 'applied' branch of this philosophical study tackles real-world moral problems. What is it?
Ethics is the philosophical study of moral phenomena. Its main branches include normative ethics, applied ethics, and metaethics.
This common long-term inflammatory airway disease causes wheezing, coughing, and shortness of breath that can flare into sudden attacks triggered by allergens or pollen. What condition is it?
Flamingo are a type of wading bird in the family Phoenicopteridae, which is the only extant family in the order Phoenicopteriformes.
Its name literally means 'Earth writing,' and it explores not just where things are but how they changed and came to be across the planet — what field is it?
Geography (from Ancient Greek geographia; combining ge 'Earth' and graphein 'write', lit. 'Earth writing') is the study of the lands, features, inhabitants, and phenomena of planet Earth.

Native to the Amazon basin, this climbing plant's coffee-bean-sized seeds can contain up to 6% caffeine — roughly double the concentration found in green coffee beans — and flavor a popular Brazilian soft drink. Name the plant?
Guarana (from the Portuguese guaran; Paullinia cupana, syns.
Never approved by any drug regulator, this THC-like compound made by hydrogenating cannabis isomers has been sold in head-shop vaporizers since the early 2020s — what is it?
Hexahydrocannabinol (HHC) is a phytocannabinoid that has been reported as a minor component of Cannabis oleoresin.
About the size of an almond in humans, this small brain region links the nervous system to the endocrine system via the pituitary gland — what is it?
Hypothalamus (pl.: hypothalami; from Ancient Greek (hup) 'under' and (thlamos) 'chamber') is a small part of the vertebrate brain that contains a number of nuclei with a variety of functions.
Serving as president of the European Commission from 1985 to 1995, this French politician played a central role in creating the European single market and laying groundwork for the euro — who is he?
Jacques Delors (20 July 1925 - 27 December 2023) was a French politician who served as president of the European Commission from 1985 to 1995.

This 20th-century Peruvian writer of mestizo descent composed novels, poems, and stories in both Spanish and Quechua, and even coined a new literary idiom to render Indigenous perspective more authentically — who is he?
José María Arguedas (Spanish) was a Peruvian novelist, poet, and anthropologist.
This American economist served as U.S. Treasury Secretary, later led the National Economic Council, and was the 27th president of Harvard before resigning a professorship there in 2026 — who is he?
Larry Summers (born November 30, 1954) is an American economist.
This Chinese computer engineer turned science-fiction writer won the 2015 Hugo Award for his novel The Three-Body Problem, and has also claimed China's Galaxy Award a record nine times. Who is he?
Liu Cixin (pinyin: Li Cxn,; born 23 June 1963) is a Chinese computer engineer and science fiction writer.

Living from about 6.2 million years ago until roughly 4,000 years ago, this extinct relative of modern elephants is distinguished by its large, spirally twisted tusks and cold-weather adaptations like a thick fur coat — name the animal?
Mammoth is a member of the extinct elephantid genus Mammuthus.
More than 80% of cases trace to asbestos exposure, and it grows from the thin lining covering the lungs and other organs — which cancer is it?
Mesothelioma is a type of cancer that develops from the thin layer of tissue that covers many of the internal organs (known as the mesothelium).
Classified by carbon count into trioses, pentoses, hexoses, and more, these colorless, water-soluble simple sugars are the basic building blocks of carbohydrates — what are they called?
Monosaccharide (from Greek monos: single, sacchar: sugar), also called simple sugars, are a class of organic compounds usually with the formula (CH2O)x.

Discovered in 1898 alongside krypton and xenon, this colorless noble gas is famous for the distinctive bright-red glow it emits, which led to its immediate identification as a new element — what gas, symbol Ne, is it?
Neon is a chemical element; it has the symbol Ne and the atomic number 10.
Founder of the charity Volnoe Delo and the industrial group Basic Element, which Russian oligarch led both En+ Group and Rusal until stepping down in 2018?
Oleg Deripaska (born 2 January 1968) is a Russian oligarch and billionaire.
Believed to have originated in Sardinia and cultivated since around the 3rd century BC, this flowering herb native to Greece and North Africa is a kitchen staple worldwide — what is it?
Parsley (Petroselinum crispum), is a species of flowering plant in the family Apiaceae that is native to Greece, the Balkans, Algeria and Morocco.
What dissociative anesthetic, known on the street as a recreational drug, can cause hallucinations, paranoia, and psychotic behavior, and is often smoked or mixed with cannabis or tobacco?
Phencyclidine (PCP), also known in its use as a street drug as angel dust among other names, is a dissociative anesthetic mainly used recreationally for its significant mind-altering effects.
Named after the American diplomat who introduced it to the US in the 1820s, this red-and-green plant native to Mexico is a Christmas staple — what plant is it?
Poinsettia (Euphorbia pulcherrima) is a commercially important flowering plant species of the diverse spurge family Euphorbiaceae.
This thorny European shrub's tart fruit flavors a British gin, while its tough wood traditionally makes an Irish walking stick — what plant is it (scientific name)?
Prunus spinosa is a species of flowering plant in the rose family, Rosaceae.
This biological process by which new organisms are produced from parents comes in two forms — one requiring a single organism, the other requiring two. What is it?
Reproduction (or procreation or breeding) is the biological process by which new individual organisms - offspring - are produced from their parent or parents.
First identified in Wuhan, this positive-sense single-stranded RNA virus prompted the WHO to declare a global health emergency from January 2020 to May 2023 — what's its name?
SARS-CoV-2 (SARSCoV2) is a coronavirus that causes COVID-19, the respiratory illness responsible for the COVID-19 pandemic that began in late 2019.
This veteran of six spaceflights was the first Russian cosmonaut to fly aboard NASA's Space Shuttle, on mission STS-60 — who is he?
Sergei Krikalev (born 27 August 1958) is a Russian mechanical engineer and former cosmonaut.

Barred from a formal education, she learned mathematics from her father's library and wrote to Gauss under the male pseudonym 'Monsieur Le Blanc,' later winning a Paris Academy prize for her work on elasticity. Which French mathematician was she?
Sophie Germain (1 April 1776 - 27 June 1831) was a French mathematician, physicist, and philosopher.
Generated in mitochondria via the TCA cycle, this dicarboxylic compound gets converted into fumarate by an enzyme that helps build ATP — which molecule?
Succinic acid is a dicarboxylic acid with the chemical formula (CH2)2(CO2H)2.
Known pharmaceutically as dronabinol, this is the principal psychoactive compound found in cannabis, used medically to relieve chemotherapy-induced nausea. What compound is it?
Tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) is a cannabinoid found in cannabis.
Following the instructions of the genetic code, which cellular process decodes mRNA outside the nucleus to assemble a polypeptide chain?
Translation (biology) is the process in biological cells in which proteins are produced using RNA molecules as templates.
This type of blood vessel usually carries deoxygenated blood toward the heart — except in the pulmonary and fetal circulation, where it carries oxygen-rich blood instead — what is it?
Vein is a blood vessel in the circulatory system of humans and most other animals that carries blood towards the heart.
This broad category of limbless, tube-bodied animals ranges from microscopic creatures to a marine species measured at nearly 58 meters long — the longest animal on Earth — what are they called?
Worm are many different distantly related bilateral animals that typically have a long cylindrical tube-like body, no limbs, and usually no eyes.

This organic compound functions as a neurotransmitter in the brain and body of many animal types, including humans. It is the chemical that motor neurons release at the neuromuscular junction to enable muscle movement. What is it?
Acetylcholine: Organic chemical and neurotransmitter. Its name is derived from its chemical structure: it is an ester of acetic acid and choline.
Born in 1929 and died in 2001, this man was a respected Saudi Islamic scholar — who is he?
This Indian economist and philosopher won the 1998 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences for his work on welfare economics, and later received India's highest civilian honor — who is he?
Amartya Sen: Indian economist and Nobel laureate (born 1933)
Comprising the talocrural, subtalar, and inferior tibiofibular joints, this region where the foot meets the leg enables dorsiflexion and plantarflexion — which body part?
Ankle: Region where the foot and the leg meet. The ankle includes three joints: the ankle joint proper or talocrural joint, the subtalar joint, and the inferior tibiofibular joint.
The clinging seed burrs of this plant genus, commonly known as burdock, directly inspired the invention of the hook-and-loop fastener — which genus?
A cousin of the tomato and potato, this European nightshade is so toxic — via atropine and scopolamine — that even handling it can harm you; its other common name is "belladonna." What's the plant?
Atropa bella-donna: Deadly nightshade, a flowering plant.

Nicknamed the 'stone' or 'house' version of its family, this adaptable mustelid outcompetes its forest-specialist, pine-dwelling cousin in open habitats — and has even gone feral in North America. Which species is it?
Beech marten: Species of carnivore. It is listed as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List on account of its wide distribution, its large population, and its presence in a number of protected areas.
Despite its name, only the soles of this tawny, spotted feline's paws are actually dark — and at just 35 to 52 centimetres long, it ranks as Africa's smallest wild feline species — what animal is it?
Black-footed cat: Small wild cat native to Southern Africa.
Rooted in prehistoric herbalism for identifying edible and medicinal species, this branch of biology studies roughly 410,000 species of land plants — what field of study?

Made up largely of the gluteus maximus — the largest muscle in the human body — these two rounded parts of the posterior pelvic region sit between the lower back and the perineum, and have long served as a target for corporal punishment?
Buttocks: Anatomical feature on the posterior of some primates.
Discovered by a Swiss chemist in 1953 and sold as Tegretol, this anticonvulsant treats epilepsy and neuropathic pain and sits on the WHO's list of essential medicines. Which drug is it?
Carbamazepine: Anticonvulsant medication. Carbamazepine, sold under the brand name Tegretol among others, is an anticonvulsant medication used in the treatment of epilepsy and neuropathic pain.
Every one of these segmented arthropods is venomous, delivering its sting through pincer-like 'legs' rather than fangs — and despite its name, none has exactly 100 of those legs — what is it?
Centipede: Many-legged arthropods with elongated bodies.
Patented in 1948, this first-generation antihistamine blocks the H1 receptor to relieve allergy symptoms like hay fever within about two hours — what is it?
Chlorphenamine: Antihistamine used to treat allergies.
Many species of this venomous snake can rear up and flare a hood when threatened — what is it?
Cobra: Index of animals with the same common name.
This common bowel condition produces hard, infrequent stools and can lead to hemorrhoids or fecal impaction, with hypothyroidism and diabetes among its underlying causes. What is it?
Constipation: Infrequent or difficult bowel movements.
Squash, pumpkin, cucumber, watermelon, and the plant behind loofah sponges all belong to which family, nicknamed the gourds?
Cucurbitaceae: Family of plants. The Cucurbitaceae ( kew-KUR-bih-TAY-see-ee), also called cucurbits or the gourd family, are a plant family consisting of about 965 species in 101 genera.
In psychiatry, this is a fixed false belief that persists even in the face of clear contradicting evidence, commonly seen in schizophrenia and manic episodes of bipolar disorder — what is it?
Delusion: Fixation of holding false beliefs.
Spanning some 40 species from oceanic to river-dwelling and ranging down to a human-sized 1.7 meters, these toothed whales are kin to belugas and porpoises — what are they?
Dolphin: Informal classification of marine mammals, closely related to whales and porpoises.

A British physicist who hauled a captured German thermionic valve back from the Western Front, he won the 1947 Nobel for mapping the ionosphere — work that paved the way for radar and shortwave radio. Who was he?

Native across the arctic and temperate Northern Hemisphere, this fern relative grows both a spore-bearing stem and a separate sterile green one, and is often mistaken for mare's tail — what plant is it?
The only member of its family found outside the Americas, this tiny insect-eating bird holds its short tail erect and is unusually polygynous for a songbird — what is it?
Eurasian wren: Species of bird. In Anglophone Europe, it is commonly known simply as the wren.
This biological process is the fusion of two gametes to create a zygote, distinct from earlier steps like insemination or pollination that merely bring the gametes together — what is it called?
Fertilisation: Union of opposite-sex gametes in sexual reproduction to form a zygote.
As commander of Apollo 8, he led the first crew to circle the Moon and earned the Congressional Space Medal of Honor — who is he?
Frank Borman: American astronaut and lunar explorer (1928–2023)

Sold under a non-proprietary name once the original patent expires, this type of medication shares the same active ingredient as its brand-name predecessor, though packaging and coloring may differ — what's it called?
Generic drug: Pharmaceutical equivalent to a brand-name product.
Bred at a Scottish estate by crossing a flat-coated gun dog with Tweed Water Spaniels, this gentle, honey-coated working dog was recognized by the Kennel Club in 1913 — which breed?
Golden Retriever: Scottish breed of dog. It is characterised by a gentle and affectionate nature and a striking golden coat.
Published in 1931 by an Austrian logician, these two results proved that any consistent axiom system for arithmetic will always contain true statements it cannot prove — what are they called?
Gödel's incompleteness theorems: Limitative results in mathematical logic.

This French mathematician, famous for his work in algebraic topology, came from an almost absurdly mathematical dynasty: son of mathematician Élie, nephew of mathematician Anna, and brother to a composer, a physicist, and yet another mathematician — who was he?
This small rodent, pointed-snouted with large rounded ears, has become the standard laboratory model organism after thriving alongside human settlements — what is it?
This physical phenomenon describes how a system's current state depends on its past history, forming looping curves in magnets and giving hard disk drives their memory — what is it?
Hysteresis: Dependence of the state of a system on its history. Hysteresis can be found in physics, chemistry, engineering, biology, and economics.
This condition restricts blood flow to tissue, starving cells of oxygen and nutrients due to causes like thrombosis or embolism — what's it called?
Ischemia: Restriction in blood supply to tissues.
This British chemical engineer founded a major chemicals group in 1998 and later became a minority shareholder with control over football operations at Manchester United — who is he?
Jim Ratcliffe: British engineer and businessman (born 1952)
Its subfamily name literally means 'large foot,' it's native to Australia and New Guinea, and a 2019 government tally counted some 42.8 million of them in harvest areas. Which marsupial?
Kangaroo: Marsupial of the family Macropodidae.

Native to the tropical Americas, this flowering shrub was carried to Europe by Dutch explorers and later brought to Goa by the Portuguese, becoming a notorious invasive weed across some 50 countries — which plant?
Lantana camara: Species of plant. Lantana camara (common lantana) is a species of flowering plant in the verbena family (Verbenaceae), native to the tropics of the Americas.
This genus of bulb-grown flowering plants, prized for their large blooms, is highly toxic to cats — even though many unrelated plants borrow its common name — which genus?
Lilium: Genus of plants. Lilium ( LIL-ee-əm) is a genus of herbaceous flowering plants growing from bulbs, all with large and often prominent flowers.
Originating in 1993 and written in ANSI C, this lightweight scripting language was designed to be embedded inside other applications — which language?
Lua: Lightweight programming language. Lua is a lightweight, high-level, multi-paradigm programming language designed mainly for embedded use in applications.
Sharing joints only with the temporal bones, this is the skull's lone movable bone, hosting the lower teeth and shrinking in size since humans began farming around 10,000 BCE — what is it called?
Mandible: Lower jaw bone. The mandible hosts the lower teeth (their depth delineated by the alveolar process).
Also known as flying foxes, these 197-plus species of fruit-eating bat likely evolved in Australasia some 31 million years ago — what are they called?
Named from Greek words for 'small' and 'head,' this congenital condition involves a smaller-than-average head size and can result from genetic syndromes or prenatal toxin exposure — what is it?
Microcephaly: Condition in which the head is small due to an underdeveloped brain.
Ranging from a tiny 8-inch species to the 10-foot Komodo dragon, this reptile genus includes an extinct relative that may have grown over 20 feet long — what are they called?
Monitor lizard: Genus of reptiles. Monitor lizards are lizards in the genus Varanus, the only extant genus in the family Varanidae.
This arthropod subphylum includes millipedes and centipedes, and one of its earliest fossils preserves the first known evidence of animals breathing air on land. What's the group called?
Myriapoda: Subphylum of arthropods. The group contains about 13,000 species, all of them terrestrial.
This Serbian-American engineer designed the modern alternating current electricity supply system—the backbone of today's power grid. Who?
Nikola Tesla: Serbian-American engineer and inventor (1856–1943)
Sold under the brand name Zyprexa, this atypical antipsychotic treats schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, and is sometimes used off-label to fight chemotherapy-induced nausea — what is this drug?
Olanzapine: Atypical antipsychotic medication. Olanzapine, sold under the brand name Zyprexa among others, is an atypical antipsychotic primarily used to treat schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.
Prized both as a delicacy and, in some species, for the pearls grown within its shell, which salt-water bivalve is this?
Oyster: Variety of families of Mollusca.
Carl Linnaeus named this crop 'hypogaea' — Greek for 'under the earth' — because, unlike most legumes, it ripens its pods below ground. What is it?
Peanut: Legume cultivated as a grain and oil crop.
Its name combines the Greek words for 'love' and 'tree,' and with over 600 accepted species it's the second-largest genus in the arum family after Anthurium — which popular houseplant genus?
Caused by viral infections, autoimmune disorders, or pulmonary embolism, this condition inflames the membranes lining the lungs and chest cavity, causing sharp pain when breathing — which condition?
Pleurisy: Disease of the lungs. Pleurisy, also known as pleuritis, is inflammation of the membranes that surround the lungs and line the chest cavity (pleurae).
Caused by a single mutation in the LMNA gene, this rare disorder causes children to age dramatically faster than normal, with most not living past their twenties — which condition?
Progeria: Genetic disorder that causes early aging.
In Euclidean geometry, which fundamental relation says the square on a right triangle's longest side equals the sum of the squares on the other two — famously written a² + b² = c²?
Pythagorean theorem: Relation between sides of a right triangle.
Rooted in Minangkabau cooking at the crossroads of the Malacca Strait, this dish slow-cooks meat in spiced coconut milk until the oil separates and it fries in its own glaze — what is it?

Nicknamed the 'dark lady of DNA,' this X-ray crystallographer's crucial contributions to the discovery of DNA's structure went largely unrecognized in her lifetime — James Watson believed she'd have won a Nobel Prize had she lived. Who was she?
Also called Besnier–Boeck–Schaumann disease, this non-infectious condition forms clusters of inflammatory cells called granulomata, often starting in the lungs, skin, or lymph nodes — what is it?
Sarcoidosis: Abnormal formation of clumps of inflammatory cells (granulomata)
About 90% of this mood-regulating neurotransmitter is actually made in your gut, where it controls intestinal movement, rather than the brain — also known as 5-HT, what is it?
Serotonin: Monoamine neurotransmitter. It is involved in mood, cognition, reward, learning, memory, and physiological processes such as vomiting and vasoconstriction.
Coined in the late 18th century, this social science studies human society — from one-on-one interactions to sweeping social structures and everyday culture. What is it?
Sociology: Scientific study of human society and relationships.

Developed in 1962 by an American pharmaceutical company and derived from a natural male hormone, this anabolic steroid treats hereditary angioedema and is unusual for surviving liver metabolism without being esterified — what is it?
Stanozolol: Discontinued steroid for heart treatment.

Nike, Inc.: American athletic equipment company.
